data.text:
Long post 🔔‼️ 🚨.  Fellow Nigerians, 
THE 3.5% RULE: How Just a Few Nigerians Can Shake the System: 
There’s a powerful truth that most of us now know:
If just 3.5% of a country’s population consistently shows up in peaceful protest, no government can stop them.
This isn’t a motivational quote. It’s based on data.
A political scientist named Erica Chenoweth studied over 100 years of movements and discovered that once a protest reaches 3.5% of the population and stays nonviolent, change is inevitable.

It has worked in Sudan. It has worked in Serbia. It has worked in the Philippines.
But can it work in Nigeria?
Let’s talk.
What is 3.5% of Nigeria?
Nigeria has over 220 million people. 3.5% of that is about 7.7 million Nigerians.
Think about it:
•7.7 million people refusing to go to work or school.
•7.7 million flooding the streets nationwide, from Lagos to Kano, from Benin to Maiduguri.
•No violence. No looting. Just pure, organized resistance.
That’s how systems fall. Not by chaos, but by unity and persistence.

Did #EndSARS reach 3.5%?
No. But it came close and showed what’s possible.
Millions were watching. Thousands marched. The world listened. SARS was “disbanded” (on paper). But because we didn’t reach critical mass, and the protests lost structure, the system recovered quickly.
The old guard just waited us out.

That’s why the 3.5% rule matters. Until we hit that threshold and sustain it, real change in Nigeria will remain out of reach.
So why is it so hard to reach 3.5% in Nigeria?
Here’s the bitter truth:
•Ethnic and religious fragmentation: Division weakens unity. One region’s cause is another’s indifference.
•Mistrust in leadership: Many fear co-optation or betrayal, as we’ve seen repeatedly.
•Government repression: Protesters are met with force, from Lekki to Ojota.
•No continuity: Movements burn bright, then fade. There’s no institutional spine to carry on the struggle.
•Tribe and religion divide us. If the protest starts in the South, the North might ignore it. If it starts in the North, the South might mock it.
•Fear: The police and army are quick to shoot. 
•Distraction and fatigue: One week we’re angry, the next week we’re dancing to #TikTok or watching #BBNaija 

These things make collective activism feel like a tall order. Still, I pay close attention to every movement that springs up in this country. I watch with hope. I give it my full attention. Because maybe, just maybe 🤔 one of them might finally strike the right chord. Hit the right nerve. Ignite something real and lasting.
I haven’t stopped believing that it’s possible. 

Has it worked in Africa?
Sudan (2019) did it. Millions of ordinary citizens, led by women, students, and unions, took to the streets. They didn’t leave. They didn’t fight. They just stayed. Omar al-Bashir, their own version of “sit-tight” leadership was forced to resign after 30 years in power.
They crossed 3.5%.

So what do we need in Nigeria 🇳🇬?
Nigeria is young. Angry. Online. Restless. Literate and Global.
We have the tools! we lack the collective discipline.
The 3.5% rule tells us that we don’t need everyone! We need; 
•A strategic plan
•Peaceful but disruptive methods
•Consistent action, not seasonal rage
•A clear message that speaks across class and culture
•7 to 8 million committed Nigerians
•Nonviolent action that’s smart, not just loud
•A united voice, not tribal, not religious
•Demands that are clear and realistic
•Leaders who don’t sell out or disappear

My Final Point: 👇🏾 
You don’t necessarily need a revolution. You need 3.5%.
When just 1 in 30 Nigerians says “we’re not doing this anymore” and backs it up with peaceful action, the country will shift.
No army, no police, no propaganda machine can stop it.
This is not theory. It’s history.
The question is: when will Nigeria’s 3.5% finally rise and refuse to back down ? 

Happy Sunday 🥰
